en: AsvGS 1.1.1: The rites pertaining to the sacrificial fires have been explained; we shall now describe the domestic rites (*gṛhya*). AsvGS 1.1.2: There are three types of cooked offerings (*pākayajña*): those offered in the fire are *huta*; those not offered in the fire are *prahuta*; and those offered in the Brahman (the Veda) through the feeding of Brahmins are *brahmahuta*.
AsvGS 1.1.3: Now they also cite a verse from the Ṛgveda:

"He who [sacrifices] with fuel-sticks, he who with oblations, he who with sacred knowledge"—even one who, full of faith, merely places a fuel-stick on the fire might think, "I am sacrificing here. Homage to him! He who [sacrifices] with oblations, he who with sacred knowledge—through knowledge alone there is indeed satisfaction. Seeing this, the seer said:
"To him who does not withhold the cow, who seeks the cow, the heavenly one, I offer this praiseworthy speech. (RV 8.74.5)
"Declare that which is sweeter than ghee and honey.
"This speech of mine is indeed sweeter than ghee and honey; let there be the sweetness of affection," this is what he says.
"O Agni, with a verse we bring to you the oblation fashioned by the heart... (AśvGS 1.1.4c).
"May they be bulls, oxen, and cows," [he says].
Indeed, these very ones—oxen, bulls, and cows—belong to him who studies this private recitation (*svādhyāya*).

"He who with reverence (*namas*) performs the good sacrifice"—by means of this salutation, indeed, for the gods do not transcend the salutation; for there is a Brāhmaṇa text which states, "Sacrifice is indeed reverence."
AsvGS 1.2.1: Now, in the evening and in the morning, one should offer oblations of prepared sacrificial food (haviṣya).
AsvGS 1.2.2: To the deities of the Agnihotra, to Soma Vanaspati, to Agni and Soma, to Indra and Agni, to Heaven and Earth, to Dhanvantari, to Indra, to the Viśvedevas, and to Brahmā.
AsvGS 1.2.3: Saying "Svāhā," one then performs the offering of the bali-oblation.
And to these very deities: to the Waters, to the Plants and Trees, to the House, to the Household Deities, and to the Deities of the Site;
to Indra and Indra’s men, to Yama and Yama’s men, to Varuṇa and Varuṇa’s men, to Soma and Soma’s men—thus [he offers] to Praditi for peace.
To Brahmā and Brahmā’s men—thus [he offers] in the center.

AśvGS 1.2.7: [He offers] to the Viśve Devas, to all beings that roam by day—thus during the day. AśvGS 1.2.8: [He offers] to those that roam by night—thus at night. AśvGS 1.2.9: To the Rakṣases—in the north.
AśvGS 1.2.10: Saying "Svadhā to the ancestors," wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he should pour out the remainder toward the south.

AśvGS 1.3.1: Now, wherever one is about to offer an oblation, having smeared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) at least one arrow’s length on all sides, and having drawn six lines—one extending northward, two extending eastward at the two ends, and three in the middle—and having sprinkled that [mound], established the fire, added fuel, swept around it, and strewn grass around it, he should perform the silent sprinkling of water from the east, south, west, and north, ending in the north.
AśvGS 1.3.2: The straining of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is performed with two strainers (*pavitra*).

AśvGS 1.3.3: Having taken two *kuśa* blades—one with an uncut tip and one without an internal node—each measuring a span (*prādeśa*), and holding them separately at their ends with the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands turned upward, he strains [the butter] toward the east once with the mantra: "By the impulse of Savitṛ, I purify thee with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya," and twice silently.
AśvGS 1.3.4: In the case of oblations of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*), the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*) may or may not be performed.

Likewise, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are performed in the *pākayajñas*. And the *brahmán* is present in all [sacrifices], except for the *dhanvantari-yajña* and the *śūlagava*. One should offer with the formula: "Svāhā to such-and-such!"
AśvGS 1.3.8: When there is no specific instruction, [the deities are] Agni, Indra, Prajāpati, the Viśvedevas, and Brahmā.
AśvGS 1.3.9: The single *barhis* grass, the fuel (*idhma*), the clarified butter (*ājya*), and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering should take place at the same time.
AśvGS 1.3.10: Regarding this, the following verse concerning sacrifice is sung:

"Having performed the *pākayajñas*, one should perform them with a single portion of clarified butter (*ājya*), a single layer of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and a single *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, even though the deities may be different. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.4.1) The tonsure ceremony (*caula-karman*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the cutting of the beard (*godāna*), and marriage (*vivāha*) should be performed during the northern course of the sun (*udag-ayana*), in the waxing fortnight (*āpūryamāṇa-pakṣa*), under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
(Regarding the tonsure ceremony:
Some [authorities] say that marriage may take place at any time.
Prior to those [marriage rites], one should offer four oblations of clarified butter.

[He offers] with the three verses beginning "O Agni, you purify our lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pavase*) and with the verse "O Prajāpati, these [beings] are not other than you" (*prajāpate na tvad etāny anya*).
Or [he offers] with the *vyāhṛtis*. Some [teachers] prescribe the combination of both.
AśvGS 1.4.7: Not some [teachers] [allow her to eat] anything at all.
AśvGS 1.4.8: "Thou art Aryaman when it concerns the maidens"—with this verse, he recites the fourth [offering] at the wedding.
AśvGS 1.5.1: One should first examine the family, both on the mother's and the father's side, as has been stated previously.
AśvGS 1.5.2: One should give a girl in marriage to a man who possesses intelligence.
AśvGS 1.5.3: One should marry a woman who is endowed with intelligence, beauty, good character, and auspicious marks, and who is free from disease.
AśvGS 1.5.4: Since the marks [of a bride] are difficult to discern, one should make eight lumps [of rice], [reciting]: "In the beginning, Truth was born first; by Truth, Reality is established."

"Whatever this maiden has been born for, let that be realized here; let that which is true be seen. Having consecrated the lumps (*piṇḍa*) with this mantra, he should say to the girl, "Take one of these. (AśvGS 1.5) If she takes from a field that yields crops on both sides, he should know: "Her offspring will be possessed of food. From a cow-pen: "She will be rich in cattle. From the earth of the sacrificial altar (*vedipurīṣa*): "She will be endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). From a lake that never dries up: "She will be endowed with all things. From a gambling ground: "She will be a gambler. From a crossroads: "She will have two husbands. From barren soil: "She will be unfortunate. From a cemetery: "She will be a killer of her husband."
Having adorned the girl, he should give her away preceded by a water-libation; this is the Brāhma marriage. A son born of her purifies twelve ancestors and twelve descendants on both sides.
When a sacrificial rite has been spread out, he should give her away after having adorned her; this is the Daiva marriage. He purifies ten ancestors and ten descendants on both sides.
"May you two perform your duty together"—this is the Prājāpatya marriage. He purifies eight ancestors and eight descendants on both sides.
Having given a pair of cattle, one should marry; that is the Ārṣa rite; it purifies seven descendants and seven ancestors on both sides.
Having made a mutual agreement, one should marry; that is the Gāndharva rite.
Having gratified with wealth, one should marry; that is the Āsura rite.
If one should carry off [the bride] while those who are asleep or intoxicated, that is the Paiśāca rite.
Having killed and split open their heads, if one should carry off a weeping woman from weeping men, that is the Rākṣasa rite.
Now, indeed, one should observe in the marriage ceremony the various local customs of the country and the customs of the village.
AsvGS 1.7.2: That which is common [to all rites] we shall now state.

AsvGS 1.7.3: Having placed a grindstone to the west of the fire and a water-pot to the northeast, and having offered an oblation while standing facing west, he should take the thumb of the girl—who is seated facing east and has taken hold of him—with the words, "I grasp your hand for the sake of good fortune," if he desires that only male children may be born to him.
AsvGS 1.7.4: If he desires female children, he should grasp only her fingers.
Desiring both [sons and daughters], he places his hand, including the thumb, at the end of her hair.
He leads her three times around the fire and the water-pot, keeping them to his right, while reciting: "I am *ama*, you are *sā*; you are *sā*, I am *ama*.
I am heaven, you are earth; I am the *sāman*, you are the *ṛc*."
"Come, let us two marry; let us procreate offspring.
Loving each other, radiant, and well-disposed, may we live for a hundred autumns.
Having led her around repeatedly, they cause her to step upon a stone: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, be thou firm."
"Endure the one who attacks; overcome the one who seeks to attack.
(AśvGS 1.7.8) Having spread [ghee] in the hollowed palms of the bride, her brother or someone acting in the capacity of a brother pours fried grain twice.
For those belonging to the lineage of Jamadagni, he pours it three times. (AśvGS 1.7.9)
Having sprinkled clarified butter over the sacrificial oblation; and also over that which has been cut off. This is the rule for the portions to be cut off.
The maidens have now worshipped the divine Aryaman, Agni;
may that divine Aryaman release this woman from here, but not from there—svāhā!
The maidens have now worshipped the god Varuṇa and Agni.
May that god Varuṇa release her from here, but not from there; svāhā!
"The maiden has worshipped the god Pūṣan and Agni;

may that god Pūṣan release her from here, not from there—svāhā! Thus, without breaking his joined palms, he should offer as if with a sacrificial ladle. Having not yet led her away, he should silently offer a fourth oblation toward himself using the hollow of a winnowing basket.
AsvGS 1.7.15: Having repeatedly poured out the fried grains (*lāja*), some lead [the bride] around; thus the two final oblations do not coincide. AsvGS 1.7.16:
Then he unties her two tufts (*śikhā*)—if they have been prepared, that is, if two tufts of wool or locks of hair are tied on the sides of her head.
AsvGS 1.7.17: With the mantra: "I release you from the bond of Varuṇa."
[He causes her to step] northward with the next verse.

Then, in the direction that is not conquered (the northeast), he makes her step forward seven steps with the mantra: "For nourishment, one-step; for strength, two-steps; for the increase of wealth, three-steps; for well-being, four-steps; for progeny, five-steps; for the seasons, six-steps; be a companion of seven steps! Be devoted to me!
May we find many sons together; may they reach old age."

Having placed the heads of both [the bridegroom and the bride] together and sprinkled them with water from a water-pot, he should have her stay that night in the house of an elderly Brāhmaṇa woman whose husband and children are living.
Having seen the Dhruva star, Arundhatī, and the Seven Ṛṣis, she should release her speech, saying: "May I find a husband who lives and may I obtain offspring."
When it is time to set out on a journey, he should cause [the bride] to mount a vehicle with the verse: “May Pūṣan lead you from here, taking you by the hand.
With the half-verse: “The stony river flows; hold fast! he should cause her to mount a boat.
With the following [half-verse], he should step out [of the boat].
AsvGS 1.8.4: [The bridegroom] should recite, "They weep for the living," when she is weeping.
AsvGS 1.8.5: They lead the wedding fire before them continuously.
AsvGS 1.8.6: At auspicious places, trees, and crossroads, he should mutter, "May the waylayers find no [obstacle]."
At every dwelling, he should have the spectators look at her with the verse, "Auspicious is this bride.
He should cause her to enter the house with the words, "May what is dear to you be fulfilled here through offspring."

Aśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.8: Marriage. Having kindled the fire and spread out the hide of a bull behind it—with the neck toward the east and the hair upward—while she is seated upon it and he has taken hold of her hand, he offers oblations verse by verse with the four [verses] beginning, "May Prajāpati beget offspring for us. Then, having eaten curd with the verse, "May all the gods anoint [us]," he should give it back; or else, he anoints their hearts with the remainder of the clarified butter.

From this point forward, for three nights or twelve nights, the two of them shall remain celibate, abstaining from pungent and salty food, refraining from sexual intercourse, and sleeping on the ground.
Or, according to the tradition that "one becomes a single seer (*ṛṣi*) after a year," they may do so for a year.
Once the vow has been performed, he should give the bride's garment to one who knows the *Sūryā* hymn.
AśvGS 1.8.13: Food [should be given] to the Brāhmaṇas.
AśvGS 1.8.14: Then he should cause [them] to recite benedictions (svastyayana).
AśvGS 1.9.1: From the taking of the hand onwards, one should personally attend to the domestic rites, or else the wife, or the son, or the daughter, or a resident pupil.
He should always keep [the fire] protected.
However, if it should go out, some say that the wife should fast.
Its times for the *prāduṣkaraṇa* (making manifest) and the *homa* (offering) are explained by those of the *agnihotra*.
AśvGS 1.9.5: And [the oblation] is for the *homa*, excluding meat.
AśvGS 1.9.6: But it may optionally consist of rice, barley, or sesame seeds.
AśvGS 1.9.7: One should offer in the evening with the formula, "Svāhā to Agni," and in the morning with "Svāhā to Sūrya"; on the second day, one should offer silently in both cases.
AsvGS 1.10.1: Now follows the *sthālīpāka* for the *parvan* (the new and full moon festivals).
1.10.2: For this, the fast is observed according to the rules of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
1.10.3: And there is the binding together of the sacrificial fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
The deities [are invoked] in a low voice, with the exception of Jāyamāna, Indra, and Mahendra. The others are for the fulfillment of specific desires.
For each respective deity, he pours out four handfuls [of grain], placing a strainer in between, saying: "I pour thee out, acceptable to such-and-such."
Then he sprinkles them with water according to how they were set aside, saying: "I sprinkle you, acceptable to such-and-such a deity.
He should cook separately those grains that have been husked and thrice-pounded;
or he may cook them together.

AśvGS 1.10.10: If he should cook the offerings separately, he should touch the rice grains while dividing them, saying, "This for so-and-so; this for so-and-so. AśvGS 1.10.11: Or, if he should cook them together, he should offer them after separating the portions. AśvGS 1.10.12: Having poured clarified butter over the cooked oblations, having removed them toward the north, and having placed them upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he should pour clarified butter over the fuel (*idhma*) and say: "This fuel is your self, O Jātavedas; by it be kindled and grow; once kindled..."
"And increase us with offspring and cattle; prosper us with spiritual luster and the enjoyment of food, svāhā! (AsvGS 1.10.13).
Having silently poured the two *āghāra* libations, he should offer the two *ājyabhāga* portions, saying: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! (AsvGS 1.10.14).
The northern [portion] belongs to Agni, the southern to Soma.
It is known: "The two *ājyabhāga* offerings are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice.
Therefore, when a person is seated facing west, his right eye is the upper one and his left eye is the lower one.
In the middle are the oblations, arranged either facing west or ending toward the west, or ending toward the east.
AśvGS 1.10.18: The portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt is taken from the north-eastern part [of the oblation].
AśvGS 1.10.19: He takes portions from the middle and from the eastern half of the sacrificial food (havis).
AśvGS 1.10.20: From the middle, the eastern half, and the western half—this is the rule for those who take five portions.
From the northern half [of the cake], he takes the portion for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Here, he does not pour clarified butter over the sacrificial oblations.
"Whatever in this rite I have done in excess, or whatever I have done here deficiently..."

"May Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make everything well-offered and well-sacrificed for me. To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the offerer of well-offered oblations, the fulfiller of the desires of all expiatory offerings—fulfill all my desires for food! Svāhā!
Thus [he says]. He should pour out the full vessel upon the sacrificial grass (barhis).
This is the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
This is the ritual procedure for the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas).
The remnants of the sacrificial oblation (havir-ucchiṣṭa) constitute the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

AsvGS 1.11.1: Now follows the ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice (paśukalpa). 1.2: Having prepared the site for the *śāmitra* fire to the north of the [main] fire, having given the animal water to drink, having bathed it, and having stationed it in front facing west, one should offer oblations with the two verses beginning "Agni is the messenger" (*agnim dūtam*), and then touch it from behind with a moist branch bearing leaves, saying: "I dedicate you, acceptable to [N.N.]. 1.3:
He sprinkles it from the front with water containing rice and barley, saying: "I sprinkle you, acceptable to [N.N.]."
Having had them drink [the water], he should pour the remainder along their right arms.
Having performed the *paryagni* rite according to the prescribed procedure, they lead them toward the north. They carry a firebrand before him.
AŚvGS 1.11.7: This [fire] becomes the *śāmitra* (the fire for slaughtering).
AŚvGS 1.11.8: With the two omentum-cooking spits, the slaughterer (*kartṛ*) takes hold of the animal from behind. AŚvGS 1.11.9: The sacrificer (*yajamāna*) takes hold of the slaughterer from behind.

AsvGS 1.11/10: To the west of the *śāmitra* fire, having quieted the animal with its head toward the east or the west and its feet toward the north, having placed a blade of grass under it before the navel, having extracted the omentum (*vapā*), having cut a portion of the omentum, having grasped it with the two omentum-spits, having sprinkled it with water, having warmed it over the *śāmitra* fire, and having carried it in front of this fire, one should sit to the south, cook it, and after circumambulating, offer it as an oblation.
AsvGS 1.11/11: In this very same fire, they cook the boiled rice (*sthālī-pāka*).

AśvGS 1.11.12: Having taken eleven portions from all the limbs of the sacrificial animal and having cooked them on the *śāmitra* fire, he should roast the heart over the spit and offer it first, before the *sthālīpāka*.
AśvGS 1.11.13: Or [he may offer it] together with the other portions.
AśvGS 1.11.14: He takes two portions from each individual limb.
They proceed with the Heart-Spike according to the same ritual procedure as before.
At a sacrifice to a Caitya, one should offer a Bali-oblation to the Caitya prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering;
however, if the deity is located in another place, this should be done by means of a messenger who is a Palāśa tree.
With the verse, "O Lord of the Forest, as you know," he should form two balls of food, place them upon a carrying-pole, and hand them to the messenger, saying to him, "Carry this offering to him.
He should say, "This for you" to the messenger. If there is any danger on the way, he should also give some weapon.
AsvGS 1.12.6: If there is a river between [the place of origin and the destination], he should cross it by means of some kind of boat or raft.

AsvGS 1.12.7: At the Dhanvantari sacrifice, one should offer an oblation to the domestic priest (purohita) between the Brāhmaṇa and the fire, saying: "O Agni, [this is] for you. AsvGS 1.13.1: In the Upaniṣad [section], [are described] the rites for securing conception (garbhalambhana), for ensuring the birth of a male child (puṃsavana), and for preventing miscarriage (anavalobhana).

AśvGS 1.13.2: If he does not perform the study [of the Veda], then in the third month of pregnancy, under the asterism Tiṣya, she—having fasted—should be made to eat two beans and a grain of barley with curds from a cow that has a calf of the same color, using a handful of curds.

AśvGS 1.13.3: When asked, "What are you drinking? What are you drinking?", she should reply three times, "The male-making rite (puṃsavana), the male-making rite. AśvGS 1.13.4: In this manner, she should consume three handfuls.
AśvGS 1.13.5: Then, in the shadow of a circular hut, he administers an unfaded herb into her right nostril.
AśvGS 1.13.6: Some [do this] with the two verses addressed to Prajāpati and Jīvaputrā.
AśvGS 1.13.7: "O thou of beautiful brows, that which is placed within thy heart, within Prajāpati... [and so forth].
"I think that knowing this, may I not incur the sin of a grandson.
(Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.14.1) / In the fourth month of pregnancy, the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) is performed.
(Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.14.2) / During the waxing fortnight, when the moon is conjoined with a masculine lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).

AśvGS 1.14: Then, having kindled the fire and having spread out the hide of an ox behind it with the neck to the east and the hair upwards, while she is seated upon it and holds on to him, [the husband recites] the two verses beginning with "May Dhātṛ give to the donor," the two verses beginning with "I invoke Rākā," and also [the verses] "O Nejameṣa," "O Prajāpati, none other than you," and "These worlds, none other than you."
Then, with a pair of unripe fruits, a three-spotted porcupine quill, and three tufts of *kuśa* grass, he parts her hair upwards, reciting "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ om" three times—
or four times. He instructs two singers, excluding the *gāthin*, saying, "Sing of King Soma."
AśvGS 1.14.7: "May King Soma protect our human offspring; may he whose wheel has settled [here], [Name]!"—thus [they address] whichever river they intend to dwell by during the fast.
AśvGS 1.14.8: Whatever aged Brahmin women who have living husbands and living children might instruct, that they should do.
A bull is the sacrificial fee.

When a son is born, before he is touched by others, one should have him eat clarified butter and honey mixed with powdered gold using a golden vessel, saying: "I give to you this portion of honey and clarified butter, impelled by Savitṛ, the source of the wealthy.
May you live a hundred autumns in this world, long-lived and protected by the deities."
Placing [his hands] upon the ears, he mutters the *medhājanana* (production of intelligence): "May the god Savitṛ bestow intelligence upon you; may the goddess Sarasvatī bestow intelligence upon you;
may the two gods, the Aśvins, garlanded with lotuses, bestow intelligence upon you.
He touches his shoulders: "Become a stone; become an axe; become unstained gold."

"O son, you are indeed named after the Veda; live for a hundred autumns! And [he recites]: "O Indra, bestow upon us the most excellent riches; grant them to us, O Maghavan, O Ṛjīṣin! (AśvGS 1.15.4). And they should give him a name that begins with a sonant, has a semivowel in the middle, ends in a sibilant (*abhiniṣṭāna*), and consists of two syllables, or else four syllables. (AśvGS 1.15.5).
One desiring stability should [use] a name of two syllables; one desiring Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*), a name of four syllables.
However, for males the names should have an even number of syllables, while for females they should have an odd number.
He should look upon the name by which he is to be addressed, and his mother and father should know it until his initiation (*upanayana*).
Having returned from a journey, he takes hold of his son’s head and mutters: “From limb by limb you arise; from the heart you are born.
You are indeed the self (ātman) named ‘son’; live for a hundred autumns. Having smelled him on the crown of the head three times, the same rite is performed for the daughter.

AŚVGṢ 1.16.1: In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) takes place. AŚVGṢ 1.16.2: [One should feed] goat’s meat if one desires the enjoyment of food. AŚVGṢ 1.16.3: [One should feed] partridge meat if one desires Vedic splendor (brahmavarcasa).
AsvGS 1.16.4: One who desires splendor [should offer] rice cooked in ghee.

AsvGS 1.16.5: He should feed [the child] food mixed with curds, honey, and ghee, [reciting]: "O Lord of Food, give us food that is free from disease and full of vigor. Further the giver; bestow strength upon our bipeds and quadrupeds."
The same procedure applies for the girl as well. In the third year, or according to family custom, the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) is performed.
To the north of the fire, he places full bowls of rice, barley, beans, and sesame seeds, each separately.
AsvGS 1.17.3: When the ceremony is to be performed later, bull’s dung and *śamī* leaves are placed in a new earthen bowl within the mother’s lap.
AsvGS 1.17.4: The father, taking twenty-one bundles of *kuśa* grass, stands to the south of the mother.
AsvGS 1.17.5: Or the *brahmā* priest may hold these [bundles].

AsvGS 1.17.6: Having stood behind [the boy] who is about to have [his hair] done, he pours together cold and warm water, or [simply] warm water, saying: "Come, O Vāyu, with water! AsvGS 1.17.7: Taking some of that [water], along with fresh butter, curd, or drops [of ghee], he sprinkles [the boy's] head three times from left to right, saying: "May Aditi shave the hair; may the waters sprinkle it for the sake of luster. AsvGS 1.17.8:
On the right side of the hair, he places three blades of *kuśa* grass each, with their tips pointing toward the body, saying: "O herb, protect him!"
Having pressed [the hair] with a metal razor, [he recites]: "O razor, do not harm him.

He cuts it with [the mantra]: "With that razor wherewith Savitṛ, the wise one, shaved the hair of King Soma and Varuṇa, with that, O Brahmans, shave this [hair] of his, so that he may be long-lived and reach old age."
Having repeatedly plucked [the hair], he gives it to the mother together with *śamī* leaves, the tips of which are directed toward the east; he places them upon cow-dung from a bull.

With the formula, "With that by which Dhātṛ shaved the hair of Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra for the sake of long life—with that I shave your hair for the sake of long life, for renown, and for well-being," he performs the second shaving.

AsvGS 1.17.13: "With that [razor] by which one may see the sun for a long time and for many nights, with that I shave you for the sake of long life, for good renown, and for well-being"—this is the third [shaving].
AsvGS 1.17.14: With all the mantras, the fourth [shaving is performed].
In this manner, three times toward the north.
He should wipe away the edge of the razor with [the verse]: "O razor, as you shave the hair with your well-fashioned, gladdening blade..."
"Do not steal his life, [O razor], while performing the purification of his head.
(ĀśvGS 1.17.17) He should instruct the barber: "While performing your work with water that is both cold and warm, do it skillfully and without causing injury.
(ĀśvGS 1.17.18) He should have the styles of the hair arranged according to the family custom.
The rite for the maiden is performed in exactly the same manner.
By this [same procedure], the gift of a cow is given.
At the sixteenth year.
In the place where the word "hair" (keśa) occurs, one should cause the word "beard" (śmaśru) to be used.
[The mantra becomes: "He moistens the beard here;
may you not steal away his life, but bring purity to his head and face."

AśvGS 1.18.6: He gives the instruction: "Arrange the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails so that they end in the direction of the water. AśvGS 1.18.7: Having bathed and remained silent for the remainder of the day, he may release his speech in the presence of the teacher, saying: "I give a boon. AśvGS 1.18.8:
A pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should prescribe [the time] for one year.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from birth,
or in the eighth year from conception.
On the eleventh day, [the initiation] for a Kṣatriya;
on the twelfth day, for a Vaiśya.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the time has not passed until the sixteenth year.
Up to the twenty-second year for a Kṣatriya; up to the twenty-fourth year for a Vaiśya. Beyond this, they become those whose Sāvitrī has been lost.

One should not initiate them, nor teach them, nor officiate sacrifices for them, nor have dealings with them. (19) The boy should be adorned, his head made auspicious, and clothed in a new garment; a Brāhmaṇa in the skin of a black antelope, a Kṣatriya in that of a Ruru deer, and a Vaiśya in that of a goat. (20) If they wear garments, they should wear dyed ones: a Brāhmaṇa a saffron-colored one, a Kṣatriya a madder-colored one, and a Vaiśya a turmeric-colored one. (21)
AśvGS 1.19.12: Their girdles are made of muñja grass for a Brāhmaṇa, a bowstring for a Kṣatriya, and wool for a Vaiśya.
AśvGS 1.19.13: Their staffs are of palāśa wood for a Brāhmaṇa, of udumbara wood for a Kṣatriya, and of bilva wood for a Vaiśya.
AśvGS 1.20.1: Or alternatively, all [staffs] may be used for all [classes].
Having offered the oblation while [the student] maintains contact [with him], the teacher stands to the north of the fire facing east;
the other [the student] stands to the east facing west.

Having filled their cupped hands with water, he pours the full [hand] of the teacher over the full [hand] of the other with the verse, "That of Savitṛ we choose. Having poured [water], he should seize his hand, including the thumb, with his own hand, saying, "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I seize the hand of N.N. (substituting the student's name).
"May Savitṛ take thy hand, O [Name]!"—thus a second time.
"Agni is thy teacher, O [Name]!"—thus a third time.
The teacher should cause him to look at the sun, saying: "O God Savitṛ, this is thy brahmacārin; protect him; may he not die. Thus says the teacher.
AsvGS 1.20.8: "Whose student (*brahmacārin*) are you? You are the student of Prāṇa. Who leads you [to me]? Whom do I lead? To whom do I entrust you? AsvGS 1.20.9:
With the half-verse, "A youth, well-dressed and girt with the sacrificial cord has come," he should cause him to turn clockwise. AsvGS 1.20.10:
Placing his hands upon the boy's shoulders, he should touch the region of his heart with the following verse.

AśvGS 1.20/11: Having swept around the fire, the student (brahmacārī) should silently offer a fuel-stick. It is known from tradition: "The silent [offering] belongs to Prajāpati; the student belongs to Prajāpati. AśvGS 1.21/1: Some, however, do so with a mantra: "I have brought a fuel-stick for Agni, the great Jātavedas.
Through this fuel-stick and through our prayer (brahman), may you, O Agni, increase; svāhā!"
Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire and touched the fire, he wipes his face three times with the words, "With splendor I anoint myself.
For it is known: "Verily, with splendor he anoints himself.
[He recites: "May Agni bestow wisdom upon me, offspring upon me, and splendor upon me."
May Indra bestow upon me wisdom, may he bestow upon me progeny, and may he bestow upon me vital power.
May Sūrya bestow upon me wisdom, may he bestow upon me progeny, and may he bestow upon me radiance.
O Agni, with that splendor which is yours, may I become resplendent.
"O Agni, with that splendor (*varcas*) which is yours, may I become splendid;

with that heat (*haras*) which is yours, O Agni, may I become hot. Having thus paid homage, having bent his knee and clasped [the teacher's] hands, he should say: "Recite, sir! Teach me the Sāvitrī, sir! (ĀśvGS 1.21.5).
Having grasped his hands with his own hands and with a cloth, he recites the Sāvitrī for him: first quarter by quarter, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole.
He should cause [the student] to recite according to his ability.
He places his hand with the fingers pointing upward upon the student's heart region, saying: "I place my vow in your heart; may your mind follow my mind.
With single-minded devotion, enjoy my word. May Bṛhaspati enjoin you to me."

Having tied on the girdle and handed over the staff, he should enjoin the student to the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*). [He says: "O religious student, drink water, perform your duties, do not sleep during the day, remain dependent upon your teacher, and study the Veda.
The period of Vedic studentship lasts for twelve years, or until the Veda has been mastered.
AśvGS 1.22.4: He should beg for alms in the evening and in the morning.
AśvGS 1.22.5: He should place fuel on the fire in the evening and in the morning.
AśvGS 1.22.6: He should first beg from one who will not refuse him.
Or [he may approach] one who does not refuse; saying,
"May you give alms," or "The rite following the study [of the Veda]."
He should inform the teacher of this.
He should remain standing for the remainder of the day.
After sunset, having cooked the *brahmaudana* rice for the occasion of the formal recitation (*anupravacanīya*), he should inform the teacher.
AsvGS 1.22.13: When [the student] has taken hold [of the teacher's hand], the teacher should offer an oblation with the verse, "The wonderful Lord of the Assembly...
(RV 10.71.1). 14: A second [oblation] with the Sāvitrī verse.
15: Whatever else may be recited hereafter [should be offered].
A third [portion] is for the Ṛṣis; a fourth is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, he should cause them to recite the completion of the Veda.
From this point forward, he shall eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, observe celibacy, sleep on the ground, and remain thus for three nights, twelve nights, or a year.
When he has completed his vow, the teacher performs the rite for the generation of intelligence (*medhājanana*).

In a direction free from blemish, he causes him to recite while he circumambulates three times from left to right with a water-pot, sprinkling a single-rooted *palāśa* leaf or a bunch of *kuśa* grass—should a *palāśa* leaf be unavailable—with the words: "O you of fair fame, you are of fair fame; as you, O fair-famed one, are of fair fame, so make me, O fair-famed one, possessed of fair fame."
"As you are the guardian of the treasure of the sacrifice for the gods, so may I become the guardian of the treasure of the Veda for men.
By this, the instruction regarding the vows, beginning with the shaving of the hair and ending with the formal entrustment, is explained.
This is for one who has not previously undergone the initiation ceremony.
Now, for one who has previously undergone initiation:
(25) the shaving of the hair may be performed or not;
(26) and the rite for generating intelligence (*medhājanana*) is also performed.
The entrustment is unexpressed;
so too is the time.
[He recites] the Sāvitrī verse: "That of Savitṛ we choose. (RV 5.82.1)
He chooses the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), whose limbs are neither deficient nor redundant, and who are [of pure descent] on the mother’s and father’s side, as previously stated.
Some say he should choose young priests.
He chooses first the Brahman, then the Hotṛ, then the Adhvaryu, and then the Udgātṛ.
Or [they may invite] all those who perform sacrifices by means of *ahīna* and *ekāha* rites.
The followers of Kauṣītaki prescribe a seventeenth assistant (*sadasya*); he serves as a supervisor of the ritual acts.
This is stated in two verses: "Him whom the officiating priests arrange in many ways... and so forth.

AsvGS 1.23.7: He chooses the Hotṛ first. AsvGS 1.23.8: "Agni is my Hotṛ; he is my Hotṛ. I choose you, N.N., as my Hotṛ"—thus he chooses the Hotṛ. AsvGS 1.23.10: "The Moon is my Brahman; he is my Brahman. I choose you, N.N., as my Brahman"—thus he chooses the Brāhmaṇ.

"Āditya is my Adhvaryu"—thus [he addresses] the Adhvaryu; "Parjanya is my Udgātṛ"—thus [he addresses] the Udgātṛ; "The Waters are my Hotrakas who invoke blessings for me"—thus [he addresses] the Hotrakas.
AśvGS 1.23.13: "The rays are my *camasādhvaryu*s," [he says] to the *camasādhvaryu* priests.
AśvGS 1.23.14: "Space is my *sadasya*," [he says] to the *sadasya* priest.

AśvGS 1.23.15: Once chosen, he should mutter: "You have spoken of greatness for me; you have spoken of splendor for me; you have spoken of fortune for me; you have spoken of glory for me; you have spoken of the hymn for me; you have spoken of what is prepared for me; you have spoken of enjoyment for me; you have spoken of satisfaction for me; you have spoken of everything for me."
Having recited: "Agni is your Hotṛ; he is your Hotṛ; I am your human Hotṛ," the Hotṛ accepts his office.
"The Moon is your Brahman; he is your Brahman, the Brahman. In this same manner, the others [accept their offices] according to their respective designations.
And when one intends to officiate as a priest, [he should recite]: "May that protect me; may that enter me; through that may I enjoy.

(AsvGS 1.23.19) The office of a priest (*ārlijyam*) should not be performed for one who has abandoned his duties, for one whose sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is too low, for one who is diseased, for one who is suffering from illness, for one seized by consumption (*yakṣman*), for one who is under accusation, or for those of "debased origin" (*kṣiptayoni*).
(AsvGS 1.23.20) He should inquire of the announcer of the Soma sacrifice (*somapravāka*): "What is the sacrifice? Who are the priests? What is the sacrificial fee? (AsvGS 1.23.21)
23. One should associate with virtuous people. 24. From the commencement until the conclusion of the sacrifice, they should neither eat meat nor approach a woman. 25.
Having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the Dakṣiṇa fire with the verse, "O Agni, grow strong by this prayer," one may proceed as one pleases.
In this manner, one who has not established the sacred fires should [perform the rite] with the verse: "O Agni, forgive this our transgression.
Having chosen the officiating priests, he should offer the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) to a *snātaka* who has arrived.
And [he should do so] for the king;
and for the teacher, the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, and the maternal uncle.
Having brought together curd and honey, [he should offer it].
AśvGS 1.24.6: In the absence of ghee or honey.
AśvGS 1.24.7: The seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, the honey-mixture, and the cow—of these, they announce each one three times.
AśvGS 1.24.8: "I am the height among my kinsmen, like the sun among lightnings."
"I now step upon this [seat] which anyone may seek to harm me. Having said this, he should sit down on a grass mat (*viṣṭara*) with its tips pointing north,
or having stepped upon it,
he should have his feet washed.
AŚGṚS 1.24.11: He should first present the right foot to the Brahmin. AŚGṚS 1.24.12: The left to the Śūdra.
AŚGṚS 1.24.13: Having washed his feet and received the *arghya* water with cupped hands, he then sips the *ācamanīya* water with the formula: "Thou art the underlayer of immortality."

AsvGS 1.24.14: He looks at the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) as it is being brought forward, saying: "I gaze upon you with the eye of Mitra. AsvGS 1.24.15: Having received it with his joined palms, saying: "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, and with the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you," and having placed it in his left hand, he gazes at it while reciting the three verses beginning with *madhu vātā ṛtāyate*. Then, stirring it three times clockwise with his ring finger and thumb, he wipes his mouth from front to back, saying: "May the Vasus consume you with the Gāyatrī metre."

"May the Rudras consume thee with the Triṣṭubh metre," [he says] on the south; "May the Ādityas consume thee with the Jagatī metre," [he says] on the west; "May the Viśve Devas consume thee with the Anuṣṭubh metre," [he says] on the north.
AśvGS 1.24.19: Having drawn up [the water] three times from the middle with the formula, "For the beings, thee. AśvGS 1.24.20:

He should consume it for the first time with the formula, "Thou art the milking of Virāj. AśvGS 1.24.21: He should consume it for the second time with the formula, "May I obtain the milking of Virāj."
AśvGS 1.24.22: "May there be milking for me from the footed Virāj"—this is the third [verse].
AśvGS 1.24.23: Not the whole [of the milk].
AśvGS 1.24.24: He should not go to satiety.
One should give the remnants of the water to a Brāhmaṇa;
if none is available, into the water;
or else, one may consume it all oneself.
Then he sips water for rinsing with the formula: "Thou art the covering of immortality.
A second time he sips with: "Truth, glory, fortune—may fortune rest upon me.
To him who has rinsed his mouth, they announce the cow.
Having murmured, "My evil has been struck down; my evil is struck down," one who intends to have [the hair] cut should say, "Do it!
Having murmured, "The mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus," he should say, "Om!"
"Release it," [he says], intending to release it.
(Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.24.33) The honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) does not consist of meat; it exists [as such].
(Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.1.1) On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the Śravaṇā rite is performed.
[The Śrāvaṇa Rite]:
Having filled a new jar with uncrushed barley-flour (akṣata-saktu) and having placed a ladle for offering the bali-oblation in a new sling, he sets them down.
Having prepared uncrushed parched grains (akṣata-dhānā), he anoints half of them with clarified butter.

AśvGS 2.1: When the sun has set, having cooked a meal of boiled rice (*sthālīpāka*) and a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) on one potsherd, he offers oblations with the four verses beginning with *agne naya supathā rāye asmān*, reciting them verse by verse. Then, with his hand, he offers the cake on one potsherd with the formula: "To the immovable one, the earthly one, svāhā! AśvGS 2.1:5: He should either leap down [into the fire] or remain with his back exposed. AśvGS 2.1:6: With the verse *mā no agne 'vasṛjo aghāya*, he makes an additional offering over it with the contents of the vessel.
AśvGS 2.1.7: With the mantra, "May the vigorous ones who partake of the oblation be auspicious to us," he offers the anointed grains with his joined palms.
AśvGS 2.1.8: He should give the other [grains] to his household members. AśvGS 2.1.9:

Having filled a ladle with groats from the jar, having gone out toward the east, having poured water on a pure spot, and having offered it with the words, "Svāhā to all the divine hosts," he pays homage, saying: "To those serpents that are terrestrial, those that are atmospheric, those that are celestial, and those that dwell in the quarters—to them I have brought this offering; to them I present this offering."

AśvGS 2.1/10: Having circumambulated [the fire] clockwise and sat down behind the *bali* offering, [he recites]: "Thou art a serpent; thou art the lord of crawling serpents. With food thou protectest humans, with cake the serpents, and with sacrifice the gods. May the serpents that are in thee not harm me who am in thee. O Firm One (*dhruva*), I entrust so-and-so to thee. AśvGS 2.1/11: "O Firm One, I entrust so-and-so to thee; O Firm One, I entrust so-and-so to thee," [he says], addressing his dependents one after another in order. AśvGS 2.1/12: Finally, he says regarding himself: "O Firm One, I entrust myself to thee."

AśvGS 2.1.13: No one should pass between [the teacher and the pupil] until the formal dismissal. AśvGS 2.1.14: "Svāhā to the serpents and the divine folk"—with these words, he should offer the bali-oblation morning and evening until the pratyavarohaṇa ceremony.
AśvGS 2.1.15: Some, having calculated [the number of days], offer that same number of balis on that very day.
AśvGS 2.2.1: On the full moon day of Āśvayuja, the Āśvayujī rite is performed.

AśvGS 2.2.2: Having decorated the dwelling, bathed, and put on clean garments, they should offer a *sthālīpāka* (cooked mess) to Paśupati and sacrifice it with the formula: "To Paśupati, to Śiva, to Śaṃkara, to Pṛṣātaka, svāhā! AśvGS 2.2.3:
He should sacrifice the *pṛṣātaka* (the mixture of curds and ghee) with his joined palms, saying: "May this be filled for me; may my fullness not depart; to Pṛṣātaka, svāhā!"
AsvGS 2.2.4: "In unison with the seasons, in unison with the ritual distributions, in unison with Indra and Agni, svāhā!
In unison with the seasons, in unison with the ritual distributions, in unison with Heaven and Earth, svāhā!"—this is the *āgrayaṇa* cooked offering for one who has established the sacred fires.
AsvGS 2.2.5: Even for one who has not established the sacred fires, it is performed in the domestic fire (*śālāgni*).
AśvGS 2.3.1: On the fourteenth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the ceremony of descending (pratyavarohaṇa) takes place.
AśvGS 2.3.2: Or on the full moon day.

AśvGS 2.3.3: Having renovated the dwelling with plastering, spreading, and covering, they should offer oblations of milk-rice after sunset, [reciting]: "O white-footed one, drive away with your forefoot and with your hind foot."
And these seven Vāruṇī offerings, and all those belonging to the royal kinsmen—Svāhā!
"Indeed, Śveta did not kill any snake in the house.
Homage and svāhā to Śveta Vaidārvya! Thus [he says].
At this point, there is no offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
AsvGS 2.3.5: Looking at the fire, he mutters: "May there be safety for us from the offspring of Prajāpati. AsvGS 2.3.6:
He should meditate mentally on the winter season while saying: "Be auspicious and well-disposed toward us. AsvGS 2.3.7:
To the west of the fire is a well-spread couch; having sat upon it and muttered, "O Earth, be pleasant," he should lie down with his family, with his head to the east and facing north.
The others [should sit] according to available space. Or, each elder [should sit] immediately after the one senior to him. Those who know the mantras should mutter the mantras.
Having gathered [the grains] three times with the mantra, "May the gods protect us from here...
(RV 1.89.6), they do so facing south, west, and north for the fourth time.
Having gathered them again, muttered the hymns to Sūrya and the *svastyayana* prayers, prepared the food, and fed the Brahmins, he should have them recite a *svastyayana*.
AśvGS 2.4.1: The Aṣṭakā rites are performed on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the winter and cool seasons;
or [they may be performed] on a single one of them.
2.4.2: On the day before, one should make offerings to the ancestors.
AśvGS 2.4.4: [The offerings are] boiled rice, kṛsara, and milk-rice;
or 2.4.5: cakes made from four śarāva-measures [of grain].
2.4.6: Having offered with the eight verses beginning "May those below rise up, and those above," or with as many as he may desire.
Then, on the following day, [the rites of] the Aṣṭakās are performed with an animal sacrifice and a cooked mess of grain.
One should also bring fodder for the oxen,
or one should burn a thicket with fire.
"This is my Aṣṭakā," [he says].
But one must certainly not omit the Aṣṭakā.

Regarding it, some call it dedicated to the Viśvedevas, some to Agni, some to Sūrya, some to Prajāpati, some to Night as the deity, some to the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) as the deity, some to the seasons (ṛtu) as the deity, some to the ancestors (pitṛ) as the deity, and some to the sacrificial animals (paśu) as the deity.

Having slaughtered the animal according to the ritual for animals, omitting the sprinkling and the formal dedication (*upākaraṇa*), he should extract the omentum (*vapā*) and offer it with the mantra: "Carry the omentum, O Jātavedas, to the ancestors where you know them to be placed in the highest realm. May streams of fat flow toward them; may all these blessings be realized—*svāhā*!
Then, from the portions of meat and the cooked mess in the pot, he recites the two verses beginning with: "O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth... (RV 1.189.1).

May the summer and winter seasons be auspicious to us; may the rains be auspicious and the autumn be free from calamity for us. May the year, our sovereign lord, grant us life; may day and night bestow upon us a long lifespan. Svāhā! May the earth be peaceful, may the mid-air be auspicious, and may the divine sky grant us fearlessness.
May the auspicious quarters, the intermediate directions, and the upward directions protect me from all sides; may the waters and the lightning protect me everywhere. Svāhā!
May the waters and the rays of light carry away our thoughts; may the Creator and the ocean wash away our sin.
May the past and the future be entirely free from fear for me; may I attain Brahman.
Sown are the syllables of the *svāra* chant, svāhā!
May Prajāpati, the Supreme Lord, swelling with vigor, progeny, and immortality, bestow them upon me, svāhā! "O Prajāpati, none other than you [has encompassed] these... svāhā.
The eighth [portion] is for Sviṣṭakṛt.
It has been stated that one should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
On the following day is the Anvaṣṭakya rite.

Having prepared a portion of that very meat, he should establish the fire on ground sloping toward the south, enclose it, and make a door to the enclosure on the north side. Having spread sacrificial grass (barhis) together with its roots three times from right to left without shaking it, he should set out the oblations: boiled rice, kṛsara, milk-rice (pāyasa), curd-mixtures (dadhi-mantha), and honey-mixtures (madhu-mantha). This is according to the ritual procedure for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
Having offered the oblations—with the exception of the honey-mixtures—he should present them to the ancestors.
AśvGS 2.5/5: For women, surā, and ācāma—this is the addition. (And ācāma. AśvGS 2.5/6:
Some [place it] in two or six furrows.
AśvGS 2.5/7: One should offer to the ancestors in the eastern [furrows].

[The rite] for women other than [the wife] is performed on the following days. By this same procedure, [the rites] from the Māgha full moon until the rainy season are performed during the dark fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada.
(Prauṣṭhapadyā?)
And month by month, one should thus establish [the offering] for the ancestors on the odd-numbered days.
One should feed at least nine [guests],
or an odd number.
AśvGS 2.5.13: An even number [of Brahmins] at rites for prosperity when [the grains have been] purified. AśvGS 2.5.14: An odd number at the other [rites].
AśvGS 2.5.15: The procedure is from left to right; barley serves the purpose of sesame.

AsvGS 2.6.1: When about to mount the chariot, he should touch the two wheels with his hands separately, saying: "I take hold of your two front feet; the Bṛhat and Rathantara are your two wheels. AsvGS 2.6.2:
[He should touch] the axle-seat with the words: "The Vāmadevya is the axle. AsvGS 2.6.3:
He should mount by means of the two right and left front [feet], saying: "By the vigor of Vāyu I mount you; by the might and sovereignty of Indra."
AsvGS 2.6.4: He should touch the reins, or if there are no reins, [he should touch] them with a staff, saying: "With the splendor of Brahman I grasp you; with truth I grasp you. AsvGS 2.6.5:
While [the chariot] is setting out, he should mutter: "O divine chariot, turn toward us, bringing thousandfold gain and booty; O tree, may you be of strong limbs! AsvGS 2.6.6:
With this same [formula], he should also [touch] other wooden objects.
AsvGS 2.6.7: With the words, "May the two oxen be firm; may the axle be strong," he should touch a part of the chariot.
AsvGS 2.6.8: With the words, "The well-protecting earth and the unassailable heaven," [he should touch] a boat.
AsvGS 2.6.9: Having circumambulated from left to right a glorious tree or a non-shallow lake with a new chariot, he should fetch branches bearing fruit.
2.6.10: Or he may go to his household fire.
2.6.11: He should approach the assembly.
2.6.12: Having murmured while looking at the sun, "Make us the highest," he should descend.
AsvGS 2.6.13: “May I be a bull among my equals,” [he says] while stepping forward.
AsvGS 2.6.14: “May we today be the favorites of Indra,” [he says] when the sun is setting.
AsvGS 2.6.15: “That of yours, O daughters of heaven, shining forth,” [he says] at the break of dawn.
Now, therefore, follows the examination of the building site.
It should be free of mounds of earth and not subject to dispute;
it should be abounding in herbs and trees.
A place where *kuśa* grass and *vīriṇa* reed are abundant;
one should uproot and remove thorny and milky plants along with their roots;
as well as *apāmārga*, *śāka*, *tilvaka*, and *parivyādha*.

AśvGS 2.7.7: Where waters from all directions meet in the middle, flow around the bed-chamber clockwise, and then flow eastward without receding—that site is entirely prosperous. AśvGS 2.7.8: One should have a food-storage room constructed on a level slope. AśvGS 2.7.9: For there, food becomes abundant.

AśvGS 2.7.10: One should have the assembly hall built on ground that slopes toward the east; it is indeed free from gambling. AśvGS 2.7.11: Young gamblers who quarrel there become prone to premature death.
AśvGS 2.7.12: Where water flows everywhere, that site is conducive to well-being and free from gambling.
AśvGS 2.8.1: Now, one should examine the site with these [tests]. 2.

Having dug a pit knee-deep, one should fill it back up with that very same earth. 3. If there is an excess [of earth], it is excellent; if it is level, it is middling; if it is deficient, it is censurable.
AśvGS 2.8.4: After sunset, one should pour out water into a vessel that is full of water.
AśvGS 2.8.5: That which contains water is praised; it is effective when moist and condemned when dry.
AśvGS 2.8.6: For a Brāhmaṇa, [the site] should be white, sweet-tasting, and abounding in sand.
AśvGS 2.8.7: [The cord] of a Kṣatriya is red.
AśvGS 2.8.8: That of a Vaiśya is yellow.
AśvGS 2.8.9: Having made that [cord] one thousand threads thick, one should measure out [the ground] as a square with equal sides according to the directions.
Or it may be elongated and quadrangular.

He sprinkles it three times while walking clockwise around it with a branch of *śamī* or a branch of *udumbara*, reciting the *śaṃtātīya* hymn; and he sprinkles it with an unbroken stream of water while reciting the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss."
AśvGS 2.8.13: One should have shelters constructed within the intervals between the bamboo poles.
AśvGS 2.8.14: Into the pits, one should cause *avakā* grass and *śīpāla* grass to be placed; for it is traditionally known that "thus he does not become a consumer of [the fire].

AśvGS 2.8.15: Having placed [the grass] into the pit of the central pillar and having spread *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing east and north, one should pour water containing rice and barley, saying: "To the Unshakable One, the Earth-dweller, svāhā!"
Then, as it is being raised up, he should address it with this mantra: "Stay right here; the Tilvaka trees have been planted around you.
O you who are full of nourishment, stand in the midst of prosperity! These malevolent ones have come upon you."
"May the young boy come to you; may the calf be born together with you.
May the enclosed vessel come to you; they have come with jars of curd," [he says] as the bamboo pole is being set up. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.9.1)
AsvGS 2.9.2: "By means of Truth, ascend the pillar, O beam, bestowing upon us a longer life-span.
AsvGS 2.9.3: Upon all four stones, he should establish the water-jar with the mantra: "Arise from the earth! AsvGS 2.9.4:
"The Araṅgara speaks aloud, bound threefold by a strap."
"He praises food (*irā*) and drives away hunger (*anirā*)," so it is said.
Now, he should pour water into this [pit] with the verse: "May King Varuṇa come with the *revatī* verses; may he stay in this place, rejoicing.
Bringing food and sprinkling ghee, may they settle together with Mitra."
Then he pacifies it.
Having placed gold into water containing rice and barley, he sprinkles [the fire] three times while walking clockwise, reciting the *Śantātīya* hymn;
and he does so with an unbroken stream of water, using the three verses beginning, "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss."

AśvGS 2.9: Having cooked a mess of food (*sthālīpāka*) in the middle of the house, and having offered oblations with each verse of the four [verses] beginning with "O Lord of the Dwelling (*vāstoṣpati*), acknowledge us," he should prepare the food, feed the Brahmins, and have them say, "May the dwelling be auspicious! May the dwelling be auspicious!
AśvGS 2.10: The entering of the house has been explained. One should enter a house that contains seeds (i.e., where grain is stored).

AśvGS 2.10.3: One should plow the field under the *proṣṭhapada* (pūrvabhādrapadā and uttarabhādrapadā), the *phālgunī* (pūrvaphalgunī and uttaraphalgunī), or under *rohiṇī*. AśvGS 2.10.4: With the wind blowing from the field toward himself, he should offer oblations or recite the mantra "With the Lord of the Field... (*kṣetrasya patinā vayam...*) verse by verse. AśvGS 2.10.5: When the cows are setting out [to graze], he should address them with two verses beginning, "May the wind blow pleasantly upon the cows" (*mayobhūr vāto abhivātu usrāḥ*).
May those cows whose udders have four openings, full of honey and ghee,
be many in our stall, yielding milk and dripping with ghee.
May they come to me, bringing delight, bearing nourishment and vital strength.
"Yielding inexhaustible milk, enter into my pen so that I may become preeminent.
And [recite] the remainder of the hymn beginning with "Those who extended their bodies among the gods" (ṚV 10.169.3–4).:
ṚV 10.169.3–4 (yā deveṣu tanvam airayanta).

AśvGS 2.10/7: Some [teachers] say that the *Āgāvīya* hymn (*Ṛgveda* 6.28) [is to be recited]. AśvGS 2.10/8: He should pay homage to the herds of cows that have not been treated with *agaru* (aloe wood): "You are beings; you are praised; you are beautiful; you are dear. May I be dear to you. Be gracious toward me; be gracious toward me. AśvGS 3.1/1: Now, therefore, follow the five sacrifices (*pañca-yajña*).

The sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to beings, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to Brahman, and the sacrifice to men. Of these, that which he offers into the fire is the sacrifice to the gods; that which he presents as an oblation is the sacrifice to beings; that which he gives to the ancestors is the sacrifice to the ancestors; that which he studies as his private Vedic recitation is the sacrifice to Brahman; and that which he gives to men is the sacrifice to men. He should perform these sacrifices day by day.
AśvGS 3.2.2: Now follows the rule for private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).

Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, having bathed in water, being purified, wearing the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītin*), having sipped water (*ācamya*), and wearing unwashed clothes, he should spread out a large quantity of *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward in a clean place. Sitting upon them facing the east, placing his left thigh over the right knee (*upastha*) and joining his hands, right over left, so that they hold the *pavitra* strainers, it is known: "The *darbha* grass is indeed the essence of waters and plants; thus he makes the sacred word (*brahman*) full of essence."
Gazing at the junction of heaven and earth, or with eyes closed, or in whatever way he considers himself composed, let him thus composed recite his *svādhyāya*.
(AśvGS 3.2.3) "Om" precedes the *vyāhṛtis*.
(AśvGS 3.2.4) He recites the *Sāvitrī* verse—first foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole verse; this is the third [recitation].

AśvGS 3.3.1: Now he should study his private recitation (*svādhyāya*): the *ṛc*s, the *yajus*s, the *sāman*s, the *Atharva-aṅgiras*s, the *brāhmaṇa*s, the *kalpa*s, the *gāthā*s, the *nārāśaṃsī*s, the *itihāsa*s, and the *purāṇa*s.

AśvGS 3.3.3: When he studies the *ṛc*s, he satisfies the deities with oblations of milk; when he studies the *yajus*s, with oblations of ghee; when he studies the *sāman*s, with oblations of honey; when he studies the *Atharva-aṅgiras*s, with oblations of Soma; and when he studies the *brāhmaṇa*s, the *kalpa*s, the *gāthā*s, the *nārāśaṃsī*s, the *itihāsa*s, and the *purāṇa*s, he satisfies them with oblations of nectar (*amṛta*).
Having studied as much as he deems appropriate, he concludes with this [verse]: "Homage to Brahman; homage be to Agni; homage to the Earth; homage to the plants; homage to Speech;
homage to the Lord of Speech; homage to Viṣṇu, the Great, I render."

He satiates the deities: Prajāpati, Brahmā, the Vedas, the gods, the seers, all the meters, the syllable *om*, the syllable *vaṣaṭ*, the vyāhṛtis, the Sāvitrī, the sacrifices, heaven and earth, the intermediate space, days and nights, the numbers, the perfected ones (*siddhas*), the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, fields, herbs, trees, gandharvas, apsarases, nāgas, birds, cows, the sādhyas, brahmins, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and all beings ending with these.
AsvGS 3.4.2: Now, the seers are the Śatarcins, the Mādhyamas, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, Bhāradvāja, Vasiṣṭha, the Pragāthas, the Pāvamānyas, the Kṣudrasūktas, and the Mahāsūktas.
AsvGS 3.4.3: [The sacrificer] wears the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).

May Sumantu, Jaimini, Vaiśampāyana, Paila, the authors of the Sūtras and Bhāṣyas, the Mahābhārata, and the teachers of Dharma; Bāhavi, Gārgya, Gautama, Śākalya, Bābhravya, Māṇḍavya, Māṇḍūkeya; Gārgī Vācaknavī, Vaḍavā Prātītheyī, Sulabhā Maitreyī; Kahola Kauṣītaki, Mahā-Kauṣītaki, Paiṅgya, Mahā-Paiṅgya, Suyajña Śāṅkhāyana, Aitareya, Mahā-Aitareya, Śākala, Bāṣkala, Sujātavaktra, Audavāhi, Mahā-Audavāhi, Saujāmi, Śaunaka, Āśvalāyana, and all other teachers—may they all be satisfied. Thus.
AśvGS 3.4.5: Having satiated the ancestors for each individual person and having returned home, whatever he gives constitutes the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
AśvGS 3.4.6: Furthermore, it is also known: whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, whichever ritual (*kratu*) he studies, by that very ritual he has effectively performed a sacrifice.
AśvGS 3.4.7: It is known that he has two occasions of non-study (*anadhyāya*): when he himself is impure, and when the place is [impure].
AśvGS 3.5.1: Now, therefore, follows the commencement of the term for Vedic study (adhyāyopākaraṇa).
AśvGS 3.5.2: When the herbs have appeared, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Śravaṇa;
AśvGS 3.5.3: Or on the fifth lunar day under the asterism Hasta.

Having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he should offer oblations of clarified butter to Savitṛ, Brahmā, Śraddhā, Medhā, Prajñā, Dhāraṇā, Sadasaspati, Anumati, the Vedic meters, and the Ṛṣis.
Then he offers groats mixed with curd.
"I praise Agni, the domestic priest"—with this one verse [he offers].

AśvGS 3.5: With the two verses beginning, “The *kuṣumbhaka* said this to him: ‘O bird, as you speak, speak auspiciously; being praised by Jamadagni, your abode is established over the entire world. O you worthy of sacrifice, come to our well-prepared sacrifice. O Agni, look upon us, look around; whether you are our own or a stranger, go as a friend of the Maruts,’ and [the verse] ‘The oblation which has been cooked for you, O King’—[these are the verses]. AśvGS 3.5:8: The single verse beginning, ‘One and the same is our intention. AśvGS 3.5:9:
The single verse beginning, ‘That we choose for the sake of prosperity and well-being.’

AsvGS 3.5.10: When about to begin the study, being assisted by those who are to be taught, he should offer oblations to these deities, then offer the *sauviṣṭakṛta* oblation, eat curd-mixed barley meal (*dadhisaktu*), and then perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*).

AsvGS 3.5.11: Having sat down to the west of the fire on *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, having placed *darbha* blades in a water vessel, and having formed the *brahmāñjali* gesture, he should mutter [the following].
AsvGS 3.5.12: Having repeated three times the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* and the *Sāvitrī* verse, he should begin the commencement of the Veda.
Likewise at the Utsarga ceremony.
He should study for six months according to the rule for a *brahmacārin* once he has returned home from his teacher.
The others [should proceed] according to the rule. Some say that he may approach his wife;
that is the rite dedicated to Prajāpati.
This is what they call the "Rainy Season Rite" (*vārṣika*).
On the middle *aṣṭakā*, having offered food to these deities, they descend into the water. They satisfy these very same deities with libations.
[He offers] to the teachers, the seers, and the ancestors.
This is the ritual for the conclusion [of the study].
Now, in place of the optional [rites], there are the optional oblations of cooked rice (*caru*).
He obtains those very desires.
Now, for one who is diseased, suffering, or seized by consumption, there is a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) consisting of six offerings with [the verse]:
"I release you by means of the oblation so that you may live. It is performed with this [verse].

AsvGS 3.6.5: Having seen an unpleasant dream, one should worship the Āditya with the two verses beginning, “O God Savitṛ, today for us...,” and with the five verses beginning, “And whatever evil dream among the cows... Or [one may worship him] with the verse, “O King, he who is my ally or my friend... AsvGS 3.6.7: After sneezing, yawning, seeing something unpleasant, smelling a foul odor, or when the eye throbs or the ear rings, one should mutter: “May I be well-eyed with my eyes, well-fortified with my face, well-hearing with my ears; may skill and wisdom abide in me.”

Having approached one who should not be approached, having sacrificed for one for whom one should not sacrifice, having eaten what should not be eaten, having accepted what should not be accepted, and having struck down a shrine or a sacrificial post—may my virility return to me, may my life return, may my fortune return;
may wealth return to me, may Brahmanic power return to me, svāhā!
May these fires that are on their hearths be established here in their proper places.
"May Vaiśvānara, increasing in strength, restrain my mind within my heart as the banner of immortality; svāhā!"— with these words he should offer oblations of clarified butter,
or two pieces of fuel wood,
or he should merely recite [the mantra].

AśvGS 3.7.1: If the sun should set while he is sleeping and free from illness, he should remain silent and not sit down; having passed the remainder of the night, he worships the sun with the five verses beginning, "O Sūrya, with that light by which you drive away the darkness. AśvGS 3.7.2: If the sun should rise while he is still asleep, exhausted from improper work, he should remain silent; the procedure is the same as above, with worship performed using the four subsequent verses. AśvGS 3.7.3: Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), constantly performing his ablutions, and remaining silent, he should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā).

AśvGS 3.7.4: In the evening, facing the north-western direction—the eighth point—he should mutter the Sāvitrī from the time the sun's orb has half-set until the appearance of the stars. AśvGS 3.7.5: Likewise in the morning. AśvGS 3.7.6: Standing and facing the east, he should do so until the sun's orb appears.

AsvGS 3.7.7: If a dove should strike against or alight upon the house, one should offer oblations or recite the mantra "O gods, the dove... verse by verse. AsvGS 3.7.8: When about to set out on a journey, [one should recite] "We [choose] thee, O Lord of the Path...
AsvGS 3.7.9: When wishing to find something lost, or when being confused, [one should recite] "O Pūṣan, together with the wise..."
AśvGS 3.7.10: [He recites] "O Pūṣan, [protect us] on the way," when about to set out upon a long journey or one that is perilous.

AśvGS 3.8.1: Now, one returning from his teacher's house should prepare these things for himself and for his teacher: a jewel, two earrings, a pair of garments, a parasol, a pair of sandals, a staff, a garland, powder for rubbing the body, ointment, collyrium, and a turban.
AśvGS 3.8.2: If he cannot obtain them for both, he should provide them for the teacher alone.
AśvGS 3.8.3: He should fetch a fuel-stick from a sacrificial tree in the direction that is not defeated (the northeast).
AśvGS 3.8.4: One who desires food, one who desires prosperity, or one who desires splendor or Vedic luster should fetch a moist stick.
AśvGS 3.8.5: One who desires both [food and prosperity] should fetch sticks of both kinds.

Having placed a fuel-stick on top [of the fire] and having given a cow and food to the Brahmins, he should perform the rite pertaining to the cutting of the hair (*godānika*). He should adapt the mantras to himself.
[He should do so] with a single *klītaka* flower.

Having bathed with water that is both cold and warm, and having put on two unwashed garments with the mantra, "You two wear fat garments," he should anoint his eyes with the mantra, "Thou art the brilliance of the stone; protect my sight.
He should fasten the two earrings with the mantra, "Thou art the brilliance of the stone; protect my hearing.
Having smeared his hands with ointment, the Brāhmaṇa should first anoint his face.
The arms [are for] a Kṣatriya;
the belly [is for] a Vaiśya;
the lap [is for] a woman.
AsvGS 3.8.15: [The bridegroom] who lives by moving his thighs [should do as follows].
AsvGS 3.8.16: He should fasten the garland with the formula: "Unharmed art thou; may I become unharmed. AsvGS 3.8.17: But not one that has already been worn as a wreath.

If they should say, "A garland," he should have it called "a wreath. Having put on his sandals with the words, "You two are the supports of the gods; protect me from all sides," he takes up the umbrella with the words, "You are the disguise of heaven. He takes up the bamboo staff with the words, "You are a bamboo, you belong to the trees; protect me from all sides."
AśvGS 3.8.21: Having tied a *maṇi* amulet on his neck with the *Āyuṣyam* hymn and having put on a turban, he should, while standing, offer a fuel-stick into the fire.
AśvGS 3.9.1: Memory, censure, knowledge, faith, and wisdom as the fifth;
sacrifice, giving, study, what has been done, truth, sacred revelation, and the vow.

"Whatever vow belongs to Agni, to Indra, to Prajāpati, to the Ṛṣis, to the royal seers, to that which has a visible form, a near-visible form, a following-visible form, a corresponding-visible form, together with gods and men, together with Gandharvas and Apsarases, along with wild and domestic animals—whatever vow of mine is within my own self, let that be my universal vow. O Agni, being one who observes this universal vow, I become [it]. Svāhā!
Thus he should offer the fuel-sticks, reciting verse by verse, beginning with "O Agni, may splendor be mine."
AśvGS 3.9.3: He should stay that night wherever they intend to honor him.
AśvGS 3.9.4: At the conclusion of his studies, having invited the teacher with a gift, or being permitted by him, he performs the ceremonial bath (*snāna*).
AśvGS 3.9.5: For him, these following observances (*vrata*) are prescribed.

AśvGS 3.9: One should not bathe at night; one should not bathe naked; one should not sleep naked; one should not look upon a naked woman, except during sexual intercourse; one should not run while it is raining; one should not climb a tree; one should not descend into a well; one should not cross a river with one's arms; one should not expose oneself to danger. For it is known: "The *snātaka* becomes a great being. AśvGS 3.10: When about to offer a gift to his teacher, he should announce his name, saying: "O Sir, here we shall dwell."
AśvGS 3.10.3: [The recitation] after the name is loud.
AśvGS 3.10.4: [The recitation] for the out-breath and in-breath is whispered.
AśvGS 3.10.5: And [the verse] beginning with "With thy mild bay horses, O Indra... [is also whispered].
Then the elder recites the verse: "O wide-extending one, I enter into you; I entrust myself to the god Savitṛ," and also [the verse]:
"O wide-extending one, through you...
Having concluded [the rite], he mutters "Om! May there be well-being! and then addresses [the water] with the verse: "The greatness of the three..."
It is known from tradition that for one who has been thus released, there is no fear from any quarter.

Upon hearing the unpleasant cries of birds, he should mutter the hymn beginning with "O you who proclaim the birth of the one who slumbers" (*kaṇikradat januṣaṃ prabravāṇa*) and also the verse "The gods generated divine speech" (*devīṃ vācam ajanayanta devāḥ*).
For a wild animal, he should mutter the verse "Praise the famous one, the youth seated on the chariot-seat" (*stuhi śrutaṃ gartasadaṃ yuvānam*).

AsvGS 3.10–11: From whichever direction he fears, or from whomsoever [he fears], toward that direction he should throw a firebrand blazing on both ends, or, having stirred a *mantha* mixture counter-clockwise, [he should recite]: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, let there be safety for me. Having encountered the enemies, burn them with your flame! Let them find neither a kinsman nor a support; destroying one another, let them go unto death! AsvGS 3.10–12:
With the words, "The wealth of both, brought together and combined," he turns the *mantha* downward.

AśvGS 3.11/(1a): From every unknown danger, one should offer eight oblations of clarified butter, [saying]: "The earth is encompassed; it is encompassed by Agni. By that encompassing, by that encircling power, whatever fear I fear from—that I ward off! Svāhā! AśvGS 3.11/(1b): "The intermediate space is encompassed; it is encompassed by Vāyu. By that encompassing, by that encircling power, whatever fear I fear from—that I ward off! Svāhā! "The sky is encompassed; it is encompassed by Āditya. By that encompassing, by that encircling power, whatever fear I fear from—that I ward off! Svāhā!"

The waters are encompassed; they are encompassed by Varuṇa. With those encompassing, warding-off [powers], whatever fear from which I am afraid—that I ward off. Svāhā! Offspring are encompassed; they are encompassed by the vital breath (prāṇa). With those encompassing, warding-off [powers], whatever fear from which I am afraid—that I ward off. Svāhā! The Vedas are encompassed; they are encompassed by the meters (chandas). With those encompassing, warding-off [powers], whatever fear from which I am afraid—that I ward off. Svāhā!
"Everything is encompassed by that Brahman; by that which is encompassed, I ward off from fear that Vṛtra of which I am afraid—Svāhā! (AsvGS 3.11/2).
Then, standing in the direction called Aparājitā (the unconquered), he recites the *svasty-ātreyam* and the remainder of the hymn beginning with "From whatever we fear, O Indra...
(AsvGS 3.12/1). When a battle has been joined, he should cause the king to put on his armor.
Having stopped behind the chariot with the mantra, "I have brought thee hither," he should offer the armor with the verse,
"Like the face of a cloud it becomes," and the bow with the following [verse].
He should cause the wife to recite the fourth verse;
he himself should mutter the fourth;
with the fifth, he should hand over the quiver.
As the [chariot] begins to move forward, he causes him to recite the sixth verse;
with the seventh, [he addresses] the horses;
with the eighth, while looking at the arrows, he causes him to recite.
AsvGS 3.12.11: While the thong is being tied, [he recites]: "Like a snake with its coils, he encircles the arm.
AsvGS 3.12.12: Then, having mounted it as it is being driven forward, he causes him to recite the *abhīvarta* hymn and the two verses beginning with "pra yo vām mitrāvaruṇā" (RV 10.174).
AsvGS 3.12.13: Then he should look at it with the *apratiratha*, *śāsa*, and *sauparṇa* hymns.
"May they uphold [the strength] of honey and ghee"—this is the *sauparṇa* hymn.
He should walk around all the directions. Having stationed himself facing either the sun or the constellation Auśanasa, he should cause it to move.
AśvGS 3.12.17: With the three-verse hymn beginning, "Quiet the earth and the heaven," he should touch the drum.
AśvGS 3.12.18: With [the verse], "Fly away, being released," he should discharge the arrows.
AśvGS 3.12.19: While they are fighting, he should mutter [the verse], "Where the arrows fly together."
AśvGS 3.12/20: He may give instructions, or he may not give instructions.
AśvGS 4.1/1: If one who has established the sacred fires should be afflicted by illness, he should move his fires toward the east, the north, or the *aparājita* (unconquered) direction.
AśvGS 4.1/2: "The fires desire a village," so they say.

AsvGS 4.1.3: Those wishing to enter the village should pronounce blessings over him, thinking, "May he be free from disease"; so it is traditionally known. AsvGS 4.1.4: Having become free from disease, he should dwell [in the village] after having sacrificed with Soma, an animal sacrifice, or an *iṣṭi* offering.
AsvGS 4.1.5: Or even without having sacrificed.
When [the ceremony] is completed, he should have a portion of ground dug up in the south-eastern or the south-western direction.
It should slope toward the south, or toward the south-east;
some say it should slope toward the west and the south.
AsvGS 4.1.9: Its length is as much as a man with his arms outstretched. AsvGS 4.1.10: It is one *vyāma* wide across. AsvGS 4.1.11: It is one span high.
The cremation ground is situated facing the open space (4.1.12).
It should be abundant in herbs (4.1.13).
As for the thorny and milky plants, it is as previously stated (4.1.14).
AsvGS_4.1.15: Where the waters flow out on all sides, that is the characteristic of the cremation ground for the cemetery.
AsvGS_4.1.16: "They have their hair, beards, body hair, and nails shaved," as was stated previously.
AsvGS_4.1.17: [The ritual requires] sacrificial grass reaching down to the ankles and clarified butter.
AśvGS 4.1.18: Here they pour clarified butter into the curd.
AśvGS 4.1.19: This is the *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter) for the ancestors.
AśvGS 4.2.1: Then they carry the fires and the sacrificial vessels in this direction.
AśvGS 4.2.2: Behind the deceased, an odd number of persons, not in pairs, and advanced in age [should follow].
AśvGS 4.2.3: Some say [he should be carried] on a wheeled seat drawn by oxen.
AśvGS 4.2.4: [He should also carry] the sacrificial cow (anustaraṇī).
A cow;
or a goat of a single color;
some say a black one.
Having tied [the cord] on the left arm, they follow and collect [the earth].
The attendants follow behind, wearing their garments over the right shoulder (adho-nivīta), with their topknots loosened; the eldest goes first and the youngest last.

Having reached that spot of ground, the performer, moving three times around the sacrificial site from right to left (prasavyam) while sprinkling it with water and a *śamī* branch, says: "Depart, go away, and creep away! (RV 10.14.9).
