AśvGS 4.2.11: He places the Āhavanīya fire in the northeast. AśvGS 4.2.12: The Gārhapatya fire in the northwest. AśvGS 4.2.13:
The Dakṣiṇa fire in the southwest.
AśvGS 4.2.14: Then, within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), he who knows constructs a layer of fuel-wood (idhmaciti).

AśvGS 4.2.15: Having spread sacrificial grass (barhis) upon it and a black antelope skin with the hair side up, they lay the deceased upon it, having carried him north of the Gārhapatya fire with his head toward the Āhavanīya fire.
AśvGS 4.2.16: To the north [of the deceased] lies the wife.
And a bow for a Kṣatriya.
Her brother-in-law, one who stands in the place of a husband, a pupil, or an old slave, should raise her up with the mantra: "Arise, O noble lady, come to the world of the living.
The performer should mutter this over a Śūdra woman.
AsvGS 4.2.20: [He recites] "Taking the bow from the hand of the deceased" over the bow.
AsvGS 4.2.21: [The procedure] regarding the *vṛṣala* has been stated.
AsvGS 4.2.22: Having strung it, and having piled up the funeral mound without piling it, he should break it and throw it into the fire.
AśvGS 4.3.1: Now he should join these vessels together.
AśvGS 4.3.3: The *juhū* in the right hand;
the *upabhṛt* in the left.
On the right side [he places] the wooden sword (*sphya*), on the left the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle;
on the chest the *dhruvā* spoon, on the head the potsherds, on the teeth the pressing-stones (*grāvan*);
on the two nostrils the two *sruva* spoons.
And having split one [of the cakes] in two;
[he places] the two portions for the *prāśitra* upon the ears [of the horse];
and having split one [of the cakes] in two.
A.ŚGṛSū 4.3.10: [He places] the vessel on his belly. A.ŚGṛSū 4.3.11: And the cup for holding the portions (*samavattadhāna*) in the *camasa* vessel.
A.ŚGṛSū 4.3.13: [He places] the sacrificial pin (*śamyā*) in his lap.
AśvGS 4.3.13: [The fire-drills] upon the thighs.
AśvGS 4.3.14: The mortar and pestle upon the shanks.
AśvGS 4.3.15: The winnowing basket upon the feet.
Having cut off one [piece],
they fill the vessels with speckled butter (*pṛṣad-ājya*). At home,
the son should prepare the grinding-stone and the muller.
A vessel made of iron or clay.
Having extracted the omentum of the Anustaraṇī cow, he should cover its head and face with the verse: "O Agni, clothe yourself in the protection of the cows.
Having removed the two kidneys, he should place them in the hands, the right one in the right hand and the left one in the left, with the verse: "Run past the two dogs, the offspring of Saramā."
He places [the heart] upon the heart;
some also [place] the two kidneys.
Some say that the kidneys are not to be used.

Having thrown all [the limbs] according to their respective places and covered them with a hide, he consecrates the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* water with the mantra: "O Agni, do not make this cup leak.

(AsvGS 4.3.25) Bending his left knee, he should offer oblations of clarified butter into the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) with the formulas: "To Agni, svāhā! To Kāma, svāhā! To the World, svāhā! To Anumati, svāhā!

(AsvGS 4.3.26) The fifth oblation is offered upon the chest of the deceased with the formula: "From him indeed you were born; may this one be born from you, for the sake of the heavenly world, svāhā! (AsvGS 4.3.27)
He gives the command: "Kindle the fires simultaneously!

If the Āhavanīya fire reaches it first, he should know: "It has reached the heavenly world"; and the son should say: "That one will succeed there; likewise, this one will succeed here. If the Gārhapatya fire reaches it first, he should know: "It has reached the intermediate world"; and the son should say: "That one will succeed there; likewise, this one will succeed here."
If the southern fire should reach [the funeral pyre] first, one should know: "It has reached him in the world of men. [One should say: "That enemy will succeed; thus shall this [son] be in him.
If they reach it simultaneously, they declare that there will be supreme prosperity.
He addresses the burning [body] with the same mantra as before: "Go forth, go forth by the ancient paths... and so on.
As it is known: "One who is cremated by one possessing such knowledge goes to the heavenly world together with the smoke.

Having dug a knee-deep pit to the northeast of the Āhavanīya fire, one should cause *avakā* grass and *śīpāla* grass to be placed therein; for it is known that "having emerged from there, he indeed goes to the heavenly world together with the smoke.
Turning to the left and not looking back, they proceed while reciting: "These living ones have turned away from the dead."

Having reached a place where water flows down, they should bathe once, offer one handful of water while pronouncing his *gotra* and name, and then emerge. Having put on other garments, wrung them out once, and cast them aside with their fringes pointing north, they should remain seated until the appearance of the stars. Or, while the sun is still visible, they may enter [the house]. The youngest shall go first and the eldest last.
Having reached the house, they touch a stone, fire, cow dung, unbroken grains, sesame seeds, and water.
On this night, they should not cook food;
they should subsist either on what has been purchased or on what has already been produced.
AsvGS 4.4.16: For three nights, they should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty.
AsvGS 4.4.17: Or, in the case of the great teachers (mahāguru), they should abstain from giving gifts and studying for twelve nights.
AsvGS 4.4.18: For ten days, this applies to the sapinda relatives.

AsvGS 4.4.19: And [one must observe impurity] for three nights upon the death of a teacher who is not a *sapiṇḍa*. AsvGS 4.4.20: And [for three nights] upon the death of unmarried women. AsvGS 4.4.21: For other teachers, [the period of impurity is] three nights.
AsvGS_4.4/22: And for a kinsman who is not a *sapiṇḍa*.
AsvGS_4.4/23: And for women who have been given away in marriage.
AsvGS_4.4/24: For one whose teeth have not yet emerged.
And [one must observe impurity] for one day when a fellow-student has died before his initiation;
likewise for a learned Śrotriya residing in the same village.
AśvGS 4.5.1: The collection of the bones (saṃcayana) takes place after the tenth day of the dark fortnight, on odd-numbered days under a single lunar mansion.
AśvGS 4.5.2: [The bones] are placed in a jar that has no distinguishing marks for a male, and in one without marks for a female.
AśvGS 4.5.3: [The assistants] should be an odd number, not paired, advanced in age, and free from bodily defects.

AsvGS 4.5.4: Walking three times around [the funeral pyre] from right to left, he sprinkles it with milk and water using a branch of the *śamī* tree, reciting: "O cool one, O thou who art possessed of coolness.
AsvGS 4.5.5: With their thumbs and ring fingers, they should place each bone separately, without making a clattering sound.
AsvGS 4.5.6: The feet first, and the head last.
Having gathered it well and purified it by winnowing, they should place it in a pit where water does not flow through from anywhere other than the rains, with the verse: “Approach this mother earth.
With the next [verse], he should scatter soil over it;
having scattered it, [he recites] the following [verse].

AśvGS 4.5/10: Having covered [the vessel] with a potsherd while reciting, "I prop up for thee," and then having returned without looking back and touched water, they should offer the *śrāddha* to him.
AśvGS 4.6/1: If [the fire] has been extinguished by the teacher or has otherwise diminished, they should perform a rite of pacification (*śāntikarman*) on the new moon day.
AśvGS 4.6/2: Before sunrise, they should carry away the fire together with its ashes and its receptacle toward the south, reciting the half-verse: "I send the flesh-eating fire far away."
Before sunrise (or before daybreak),
having placed it at a crossroads or wherever they walk three times around it counter-clockwise, with their left hands and striking their left thighs.

AśvGS 4.6: Then, having returned without looking back, having touched water, and having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, they should prepare new water-jars (*maṇika*), pitchers (*kumbha*), and vessels for sipping water; *śamī* flowers and garlands; a fuel-stick (*idhma*) made of *śamī*, two kindling-boards (*araṇī*), and enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *śamī*; bull’s dung, a hide, fresh butter, a stone, and as many bunches of *kuśa*-grass as there are young women.
AśvGS 4.6:5: At the time of the fire-ritual, one should produce the fire with the half-verse: "Right here let this other Jātavedas be born."
They remain sitting while lighting that [fire] until the night has subsided, reciting discourses on long life, proclaiming auspicious things, and narrating the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*.

(AśvGS 4.6.6) When the sounds have ceased or when they have entered the house or the dwelling, one should carry an unbroken stream of water, starting from the right side of the door and proceeding as far as the north, with the mantra: "Stretching the thread, follow the light of the mid-region" (*tantum tanvan rajasobhānum anvihi*). (AśvGS 4.6.7)

Then, having kindled the fire and spread out the hide of a bull behind it—with the neck to the east and the hair upwards—he should make his dependents mount it [with the words]: "Mount it, choosing long life unto old age.
He should place the enclosing sticks around [the fire with the words]: "I set up this enclosure for the living."

Having placed a stone to the north of the fire with the verse, "May they place death within by means of the mountain," and having offered oblations verse by verse with the four verses beginning, "Go away, O Death, along your own path," he should look at his kinsmen with the verse, "As the days follow one another in succession.

The young women, each separately, using two blades of fresh *darbha* grass held in their hands, should apply fresh butter to their eyes with their thumbs and ring fingers. Turning away, they should cast the [grass] aside.
He should look at those applying the ointment with the verse, "These women, not widows, having good husbands..."
AśvGS 4.6.13: With the mantra, "The stony river flows; hold fast," the maker [of the altar] should first touch the stone.
AśvGS 4.6.15: They cite that a tawny ox should be led around.
AśvGS 4.6.17: Then they sit down where they intend to remain, having covered themselves with a new, unwashed garment.
They remain sitting without sleeping until sunrise.

When the sun has risen, having recited the hymns dedicated to Sūrya and the *svastyayana* (auspicious) prayers, and having prepared the food, he should offer oblations verse by verse with the mantra, "May our sin be burned away" (*apa naḥ śośucad agham*), feed the Brāhmaṇas, and have them pronounce a blessing.
A cow, a bronze vessel, and a new garment constitute the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Now, therefore, regarding the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha—whether it be for a specific desire (*kāmya*), for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), or for a single ancestor (*eka-uddiṣṭa*).

Having invited Brāhmaṇas endowed with learning, good character, and right conduct—or at least one—having informed them of the time, and having seen them bathed, performed the purification of their feet, and sipped water (*ācamana*), he should seat them facing north as representatives of the ancestors, assigning one to each ancestor, or two, or three.
In the case of a rite for prosperity (*vṛddhi*), there is an abundance of fruit.

But one [offering] alone is by no means sufficient for all [the ancestors]. (AśvGS 4.7.4) At the first [offering], it is optional. (AśvGS 4.7.5) This is explained by the rules regarding the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). (AśvGS 4.7.6)
Having offered water;
having offered a seat made of double-folded *darbha* grass;
having offered water.

AŚGṚS 4.7/10: Having poured water into three vessels made of metal, stone, or clay—either containing the same substance or each containing a different one—and having placed *darbha* grass within them;

AŚGṚS 4.7/11: After consecrating the water with the mantra, "May the goddesses be for our aid," he pours sesame seeds into them with the formula: "Thou art sesame, whose deity is Soma, created by the gods at the *gosava* sacrifice.
Offered by the ancients, do thou, through the *svadhā* offering, gratify these ancestors and these worlds for us; *svadhā*, obeisance!"*

AśvGS 4.7.13: With the right hand, using the space between the thumb and forefinger of the other hand—because he is wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder—or with the left hand supported by the right, [he offers] as follows, without prior [formula]: "O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*. AśvGS 4.7.14:

When he is about to cause them to accept those [waters], he says once for each: "The *arghya* waters, *svadhā*! AśvGS 4.7.15: Once they have been released, he should recite the following consecration formula: "Those divine waters which have arisen from the earth, those which are in the intermediate space, and those which are terrestrial..."
"Golden-hued, worthy of sacrifice, may those waters be auspicious and pleasant for us. Having poured together the remnants of the offerings, he who desires a son anoints his face with that water.
(Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 4.7.16) One should not lift up first the vessel of the ancestors from which the *arghya* was offered;
Śaunaka has said that the ancestors remain there, enveloped [by the scent].
At this time, there is the offering of perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and garments.

Having taken up food smeared with ghee, he asks for permission, saying, "I shall perform the fire-rite" (*agnau kariṣye*), or "I will perform it" (*karavai*), or "I am performing it" (*karavāṇi*). The response is, "Let it be done," (*kriyatām*), or "Do it" (*kuruṣva*), or "Perform it" (*kuru*).
AśvGS 4.7.20: Then he offers oblations in the fire as previously described.
AśvGS 4.7.21: Or, having obtained permission, [he may offer] directly into the hands [of the Brahmins].
AśvGS 4.7.22: "The gods have the fire as their mouth; the ancestors have the hands as their mouth," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
AsvGS 4.7.23: If, after they have rinsed their hands, he offers them other food;
4.7.24: "Food upon food";
4.7.25: "May what is released and given be successful."

AsvGS 4.7.26: Knowing them to be satiated, he should cause them to hear the verses containing the word "honey" (*madhumatī*) and [the verse] beginning with "They have eaten, they have rejoiced" (*akṣann amīmadanta*).

AsvGS 4.7.27: Having asked, "Is it completed? (*sampannam*), he should set aside for the sake of the *piṇḍas* whatever food has been consumed, together with the contents of the cooking pot; he should then present the remainder. AsvGS 4.7.28: Whether [the guests] have expressed their approval or not, he should place the *piṇḍas* after they have finished eating but before they have sipped water for purification (*anācānteṣu*).
AśvGS 4.7.29: Some [teachers say that the rite is completed] when they have sipped water.
AśvGS 4.7.30: Having scattered food and put on the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, he should dismiss them with the words, "Om, let the svadhā be uttered.
AśvGS 4.7.31: Or [he may dismiss them] with the words, "Let there be svadhā."
AśvGS 4.8.1: Now follows the rite of the spit-ox (śūlagava).
AśvGS 4.8.2: It is performed in autumn or spring with a living calf.
AśvGS 4.8.3: [The animal] must be the best of its own herd.
A black-spotted deer with white spots;
some say it should be dappled.
It may be black at will, provided it has copper-colored hooves.
Having sprinkled [him] with water containing rice and barley,
from the head down to the feet,
[he says]: "O beloved one, grow for Rudra, the Great God."
One should cause it to grow until its teeth have fully emerged, or until it has become a bull. This should be done in a direction auspicious for sacrifice,
out of sight from the village.
AśvGS 4.8.13: After midnight. AśvGS 4.8.14: Some say, "at sunrise.

AśvGS 4.8.15: Having seated a learned and virtuous Brahmin as the *brahmán*, having driven in a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) consisting of a fresh branch with leaves, and having wound two creepers or two *kuśa*-ropes as cords around it—one around the middle of the post and the other around the head of the animal—he binds the animal either to the post or to the cord with the formula: "To whom [obeisance], to him I bind you, the one dear to him."
AśvGS 4.8.16: The rites beginning with the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) are the same as those for the animal sacrifice (paśu).
AśvGS 4.8.17: We shall state the specific differences.
AśvGS 4.8.18: It is known from tradition that one should offer the omentum (vapā) either with a vessel or with a palāśa leaf.
AśvGS 4.8.19: “To Hara, Mṛda, Śarva, Śiva, Bhava, Mahādeva, Ugra, Bhīma, Paśupati, Rudra, Śaṅkara, and Īśāna, svāhā! AśvGS 4.8.20:
Or with the next six [mantras].
AśvGS 4.8.21: Or simply, “To Rudra, svāhā!”

AśvGS 4.8.22: He should offer an oblation on four bundles of *kuśa* grass in the four directions with the formula: "O Rudra, those armies of yours which are in the eastern direction—to them be this salutation; do not harm me. In this manner, the assignment is performed for each direction.
AśvGS 4.8.23: With four hymns he should worship the four directions: "What [is] for Rudra," "These [prayers] for Rudra," "To thee, O Rudra," and "Father, to Rudra, whose bow is firm."
AśvGS 4.8.25: He should throw the husks, the chaff, the tail, the hide, the head, and the feet into the fire.
AśvGS 4.8.26: "He should make a mat from the hide," says Śāṃvatya.

AśvGS 4.8.27: To the north of the fire, he should pour out the blood upon mats of *darbha* grass or on bundles of *kuśa* grass with the words: "O hissing, roaring, gathering, and spreading serpents, whatever belongs to you here, take that!"

AśvGS 4.8/28: Then, having turned toward the north, [he offers with the formula]: "O hissing, roaring, scattering, and spreading serpents, take away whatever belongs to you here! The serpents take away whatever blood or internal organs (ūvadhyam) have flowed out there.
AśvGS 4.8/29: "Indeed, he who knows thus pleases the sacrificer by saying: 'All his names, all his armies, and all his elevations [are his].
AśvGS 4.8/30: "It is known: 'He does not harm even one who speaks against him.'"
AśvGS 4.8.31: One should not eat of it.
AśvGS 4.8.32: They should not bring it into the village; for this god is prone to attack people.
AśvGS 4.8.33: He should keep his attendants away from the vicinity.
But at the command [of the officiant], he should eat it, saying, "For well-being.
This Śūlagava sacrifice brings wealth, secures the world, is meritorious, grants sons, is favorable for cattle, bestows long life, and confers fame.
Having performed this sacrifice, one should release another [bull].
AsvGS_4.8/39: Reciting the Śaṃtātīya hymn, he should go home.
AsvGS_4.8/40: In the event of affliction among the cattle, he should sacrifice to this very same deity in the middle of the cow-pen.
AsvGS_4.8/41: He should offer a cooked mess of food as a complete oblation.
AśvGS 4.8.42: Having thrown the sacrificial grass and the clarified butter into the fire, he should drive the cows back while smoke is still rising.
AśvGS 4.8.43: Reciting the Śaṃtātīya hymn, he should go into the midst of the cattle. AśvGS 4.8.44: Homage to Śaunaka! Homage to Śaunaka!
